session01.section: Introduction and Section 10.7; PDF pages 1–2 and 34–35
session01.purpose: Names the six LLM research applications and distinguishes exact replay from claim-level replication while specifying a minimum research record.
Provides a social-science framework for measurement, prompting and simulation.
Shows how generative AI is entering sociological research and where disciplinary judgment remains necessary.
Turns general transparency concerns into fields a researcher can actually save.
Explains why model access and versioning complicate conventional replication.

session02.purpose: Introduces annotation, validation and the weakening of an unquestioned human gold standard.
Connects established coding decisions to prompt design.
Treats semantically similar prompt variants as a reliability problem.
Locates zero-shot classification among other ways of adapting a model.
Connects annotation performance to downstream social-science use.

session03.purpose: Defines the validation problem for annotation, providing a boundary case against which qualitative interpretation can be distinguished.

session03.section: Open coding, focused coding and memo-writing
session03.purpose: Establishes qualitative analysis as iterative movement between data and theoretical ideas.
Shows a researcher–LLM–researcher process for qualitative coding.
Makes the chatbot interaction itself part of the methodological account.
Provides a recent empirical case in which humans retained the interpretive analysis.

session04.purpose: Treats text, images and video as annotatable material and states the corresponding validation problem.
Shows how professional communities organize what becomes visible as evidence.
Supplies a sociological account of sequence and emotional entrainment in violent situations.
Explains how video sequence analysis turns recorded action into analyzable data.
Introduces the technical debate over what text-only models lack about embodied experience.

session05.purpose: Connects generated treatments to construct validity and experimental control.
Places generated vignettes within the sociology of factorial survey design.
Explains why two differently worded treatments may change more than the intended construct.
Provides a published example of generated policy messages tested on human participants.
Shows how candidate questions can be selected adaptively without treating generation as validation.

session06.purpose: Locates adaptive interviewing between treatment generation and tool-augmented data collection.
Supplies foundational criteria for specificity, range, depth and personal context.
Provides a major contemporary implementation of AI-led interviews.
Shows how a qualitative chatbot was built and how researchers experienced it.
Provides a comparison between adapting a survey and composing a qualitative probe.

session07.purpose: Distinguishes uses of silicon sampling and their validation targets.
Frames artificial stand-ins as representations with specific inferential limits.
Tests how generative models answer survey questions and where their distributions differ.
Shows how synthetic substitutes can flatten within-group heterogeneity.
Previews a different target: predicting unasked opinions for observed respondents.

session08.purpose: Links different synthetic-data uses to different standards of validation and replication.
Uses observed survey answers to predict missing responses for actual respondents.
Separates resemblance on one statistic from broader population realism.
Tests prediction of experimental results rather than replacement of individual participants.
Provides a hard case for claims that missing social worlds have been recovered.

session09.purpose: Introduces generative agent-based models and their specification problems.
Establishes the explanatory logic of moving from actor rules to macro patterns.
Adds memory, reflection and planning to language-model agents.
Shows how interaction structure and model policies jointly shape opinion dynamics.
Provides an empirical bridge to convention formation in Week 10.

session10.purpose: Frames emergence and validation in generative simulations.
Tests social convention formation in populations of language-model agents.
Shows why apparently emergent behavior can be indistinguishable from inherited or leaked solutions.
Examines whether debate among reasoning agents improves collective outcomes.
Provides an alternative design for attributing macro outcomes to interaction.

session11.purpose: Defines tool-augmented data collection and the centrality of provenance.
Provides an end-to-end research automation case and a demanding long-horizon benchmark.
Makes responsibility and transparency explicit when multiple agents contribute.
Provides concrete fields that can be carried into an agent provenance record.

session12.purpose: Summarizes the new replication problem created by changing models and services.
Specifies what behavioral-science articles should report about LLM use.
Distinguishes rerunning a workflow from reproducing a model-mediated result.
Extends replication questions to multi-agent ownership and responsibility.

session13.purpose: Treats LLMs as socially consequential objects rather than neutral research instruments.
Shows how state media environments are associated with patterned model outputs.
Examines the relationship between model outputs and creator geography or ideology.
Raises a higher evidentiary threshold for claims about model self-reports and human values.
Provides a survey-based audit whose claims can be compared with cultural explanations.
